title: Which God Do You Turn To When Food Might Run Short? — Cross-Cultural Food-Worry Horizons, Moralistic vs. Local Deities & Christchurch Earthquake Panels

teenKit.tldr: When human survival is threatened by extreme food scarcity, our brains don't just get generically "more religious." Instead, we dynamically shift which type of deity we lean on—swapping local spirits for vast, moralistic enforcers.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding how our minds handle survival panic reveals deep evolutionary hacks that still secretly shape how we trust strangers, build societies, and panic during crises today.
keyTakeaways: Material insecurity—like not knowing where your next meal is coming from—actively rewires human religious cognition and behavior.
Cross-cultural data from 14 populations shows that food worry specifically drives people toward punishing, moralistic deities rather than local spirits.
Disaster studies, like the Christchurch earthquake research, allow scientists to track these psychological shifts in real-time longitudinal panels.

vocab.meaning: A supreme, all-knowing god who cares deeply about human rules, fairness, and punishing bad behavior across entire societies.
A smaller, community-bound spirit, ancestor, or nature god tied to a specific place, family, or immediate geography.
The raw, stressful state of lacking predictable access to basic physical survival needs like food, water, and shelter.
A scientific research study that tracks the exact same group of people over a long period to see how their lives and minds change.

quiz.question: According to the research discussed, what happens to human religious commitment when severe food scarcity hits?
options: People completely abandon all religious beliefs overnight.
People shift their focus toward moralistic deities rather than local spirits.
Everyone automatically converts to the exact same global religion.
Religious commitment decreases entirely because people are too stressed to care.
quiz.explanation: Data across multiple cultures shows that food insecurity specifically predicts a greater lean toward moralistic gods rather than local ones.

quiz.question: What is the primary difference between a local deity and a moralistic deity as defined in this research?
options: Local deities are only fictional, while moralistic deities are scientifically proven.
Moralistic deities are tied to local geography, while local deities watch over entire planets.
Local deities are usually tied to specific places or communities, whereas moralistic deities enforce broad ethical rules across societies.
There is no difference; researchers use the terms interchangeably.
quiz.explanation: Local deities are embedded in specific local contexts or lineages, while moralistic deities police universal human morality and social cooperation.

quiz.question: Why did researchers study the aftermath of the Christchurch earthquake (Sibley & Bulbulia 2012)?
options: To figure out how to build earthquake-proof houses using ancient religious rituals.
To test how a sudden catastrophic natural disaster and material disruption impacts human psychology and beliefs in real-time.
To prove that earthquakes are caused by angry moralistic gods.
To measure how much food was lost in local grocery stores.
quiz.explanation: Longitudinal panels during natural disasters like Christchurch give scientists a rare window to track how sudden trauma and insecurity alter human thought patterns.
